title: A Harbor for the Typewriter
premise: In 1949, Quentin Ishikawa carries diplomatic codes for a republic collapsing under coup and siege, hiding her identity behind the neutral role of courier. When a sealed letter entrusted to her names the family of the typist she has quietly loved for years as targets of the coming regime, Quentin must choose between delivering the mission's final dispatch — which will save her own escape — or diverting the workshop's people to safety first. She spends the last days of the republic forging documents, smuggling the family out in pieces, and discovering that the silences she mastered were never protection, only delay. The book ends with the workshop burning behind them, the letter finally opened and read aloud on a refugee ship, and Quentin choosing to sign her true name at last.
about_author: Lior Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing displaced-persons records from postwar Europe. Their fiction is drawn from the marginalia of those files — the notes, aliases, and unsent letters left between official lines.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In the besieged capital, Quentin receives the mission's final sealed letter and memorizes the codes it contains, noting the courier seal is broken and re-glued by someone else. She delivers routine dispatches through checkpoints, passing the typefoundry where Mara Voss works. Emotional beat: disciplined calm stretched over dread; something has already gone wrong before the story begins.

chapters.title: Which Silences Keep People Safe
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, with a flashback to 1929 when she first learned to erase her name and heritage to survive. Present-day: she visits the workshop under pretext of repairing a portable typewriter, watching Mara set type with her father and brother. Emotional beat: tenderness measured out in small, deniable gestures; the cost of twenty years of concealment made intimate.

chapters.title: A Letter That Names Them
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Alone, she steams open the damaged final letter to verify its contents and finds a list: the Voss family is named among those to be detained when the regime consolidates. Her own extraction depends on delivering this same dispatch. Emotional beat: vertigo — duty and love revealed as irreconcilable, the premise's central trap sprung.

chapters.title: The Workshop Still Stands
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Through Mara's eyes we see the foundry's last ordinary days: casting sorts, joking about the shelling, her father refusing to believe the lists are real. Mara notices Quentin's visits have changed — the courier lingers, asks strange questions. Emotional beat: warmth on the edge of catastrophe; dramatic irony as readers know what the family doesn't.

chapters.title: Forged in Lead
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She begins forging exit papers using the workshop's own type, trading favors with a corrupt border clerk, and lying to her handler about the letter's condition. Each forgery is a small treason against the mission. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into recklessness; love converting duty's machinery against itself.

chapters.title: What the Handler Knows
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, intercut with her handler Aldric's. Aldric suspects the tampering and offers Quentin a bargain: deliver the letter intact and he'll look away from everything else. He reveals he knows who she really is — the name she buried in 1929. Emotional beat: exposure; the past weaponized, identity no longer hers alone to keep.

chapters.title: Moving Pieces
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The exodus begins in fragments — the father first with the matrices, the brother overland, each leg threatened by checkpoints and informants. Mara, now told part of the truth, helps forge her own family's papers and confronts Quentin about what she withheld. Emotional beat: found family forged under pressure; trust built from confessed lies.

chapters.title: The Last Dispatch
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Cornered by Aldric at the harbor, Quentin must hand over the letter to secure the ship's departure papers for the Vosses. She gives him the codes but substitutes a decoy page inside the seal — gambling that the mission dies so the family lives. Emotional beat: climax of sacrifice; she surrenders the self that duty built.

chapters.title: Fire and Type
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. As troops enter the city, the workshop is torched; Mara and Quentin make the quay through smoke and crowds, carrying only a case of type and the opened letter. Aldric, holding the decoy, lets them board — one silence returned. Emotional beat: grief and release entwined; the old world burning as something new is carried out of it.

chapters.title: Her True Name
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, epilogue aboard the refugee ship. At dawn Mara reads the letter aloud — it is half mission, half confession, written by someone who once chose love over duty too. Quentin signs the passenger manifest with the name she buried in 1929, then writes a second line: Mara Voss. Emotional beat: resolution; identity reclaimed, silence ended, a harbor found in a person rather than a place.
